question.text: Which type of Power of Attorney remains valid even if the grantor becomes mentally incapacitated?

explanation.text: The Logic: A Durable Power of Attorney is a POA that, by its express terms, remains valid even after the grantor becomes mentally incapacitated. An ordinary (non-durable) POA generally lapses on the grantor's incapacity, because the grantor must continue to be legally competent for the agent's authority to subsist. The Trap: A General Power of Attorney (Option A) confers broad authority on the agent but is not specifically designed to survive the grantor's incapacity. A Special Power of Attorney (Option B) is limited in scope to specific acts. A Temporary Power of Attorney (Option D) is limited in time and does not extend through incapacity. Note: The "Durable" Power of Attorney concept and the rule that an ordinary POA becomes invalid on incapacity are not defined in the cited NISM Series XVII Retirement Adviser Certification Examination Workbook (June 2025 version) pages 215-216 or 219. The workbook defines General POA and Specific POA and notes that an already executed POA can help when the grantor is unable or mentally incapacitated, without using the term "Durable POA". The framing above reflects general legal/estate-planning knowledge.
